On the other hand, Mr Mohammad Ismail, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, submits that notice has been legally served upon the tenant-petitioner in view of his receipt of the photo copy of the notice by putting his signature thereon. It is submitted by him further that by not disowning the signature specifically in the written statement, the tenant is estopped in raising the plea of non-service of notice under section 106 of The Transfer of property Act during the trial. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate that since the envelop containing the notice under section No. 106 of The Transfer of property Act was duly registered and posted in the correct address of the tenant petitioner, usual presumption is that notice was duly served. He then submits that the compensation as awarded by the trial Court is in accordance with law. He, thus, supports the judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge and has referred to certain decisions to be discussed herein below. 

 11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner refers to the case of Hajee Khabiruddin Ahmed vs Salam Kabir reported in 34 DLR (AD) 271. In this case similar question arose as to the presumption of service of notice when a registered letter was proved to have been duly addressed and posted. With regard to the question of due service of notice upon the tenant under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act, their Lordships in the Appellate Division with reference to the provisions of section 27 of the General Clauses Act, held as follows: 

 “The provision of section 27 did not leave any scope for drawing any adverse presumption regarding service of notice. in case of a letter sent by registered post according to these provisions, as soon as the posting by registered post of a properly addressed letter containing any notice or document to be served by post is proved, such service of notice shall, be deemed to have been effected after the lapse of a reasonable time."
